narrative: The model estimates a 63% chance that you will leave your job. In this promotion decision, that elevated leave risk is why you are denied: the prediction treats you as more likely than not to depart, so the organization is reluctant to award a promotion. The strongest signal was your overall years of experience. At 6–10 years, you sit above the most common range among employees predicted to stay, where about half have only 1–5 years, and this pushed the prediction toward leaving. Second was your time in your current organization: 1–5 years is common among stayers, yet in your profile it still added to the leave signal. Third was having other job opportunities. That matters because only about 23% of employees predicted to stay reported outside opportunities, while your yes answer pushed strongly toward leaving. So all three leading factors increased, rather than reduced, the estimated likelihood of departure. Next, you and the organization should discuss retention directly: whether the promotion path, recognition, development, and workload feel sustainable, and whether external opportunities are making you consider leaving. A clear conversation about career progression, support, and engagement would help test whether the 63% risk can be reduced before future promotion decisions.
